title: Travelling in mainland China with a Dutch passport
recommendation: Decision for the app: travel facts are dated reference cards, not learning content. Every card shows 'checked 2026-11-02', its official link and a recheck-by date, and is hidden or flagged once past that date. Ship only 'verified' items as facts: visa-free 30 days until 2026-12-31 (travel-facts.visa-free-netherlands, travel-facts.visa-free-rules); online arrival card (travel-facts.online-arrival-card); 24-hour accommodation registration with the online NIA route since 2026-09-21 (travel-facts.accommodation-registration-rule, travel-facts.accommodation-registration-online); payments (travel-facts.payments-foreign-cards, travel-facts.payments-verification-limits, travel-facts.payments-fees); cash (travel-facts.cash); trains (travel-facts.trains-12306-registration, travel-facts.trains-arrival-time, travel-facts.trains-e-tickets); emergency numbers 110 police, 119 fire, 120 ambulance (travel-facts.emergency-numbers; show 122 only as 'traffic accidents, to verify'); 240-hour transit as the fallback if the visa-free policy lapses (travel-facts.240-hour-transit); blocked services and Dutch travel advice (travel-facts.internet-blocked, travel-facts.dutch-travel-advice). Show the 'disputed' gate question (travel-facts.trains-gates-passport) as 'varies by station: use the staffed lane 人工通道 if the gate refuses your passport'. Keep the 'unverified' items (122's service, Dutch embassy and consulates, VPN, roaming/eSIM, maps/taxi/dictionary apps, TourCard, the passport-carrying law article, the 2026 entry provisions, hosting and CDN blocks) out of the app, or label them 'to verify', until they are checked on https://www.nederlandwereldwijd.nl/reisadvies/china or, for Chinese law, on flk.npc.gov.cn. Advice that is safe without the law citation: always carry your passport, because it is your train ticket and hotels must register you. The visa-free card needs a hard expiry of 2026-12-31 (travel-facts.visa-free-end-date-watch), with a re-check in November-December 2026. Because Google services are blocked in China (travel-facts.internet-blocked) and GFWList also lists vercel.app, netlify.app, github.io, githubusercontent.com, jsdelivr.net, claude.ai and anthropic.com (travel-facts.internet-blocked-app-hosting, unverified), the PWA must not depend on Google-hosted fonts, APIs or TTS, CDN scripts or AI APIs for core features, and must work fully offline once installed. The learner should install it and let it cache everything before leaving. If it must also open inside China, test the domain from China first; a custom domain is a better bet than *.vercel.app (inference). Vocabulary hooks: these terms appeared in official Chinese sources this session; pinyin and tones still need checking against CC-CEDICT: 住宿登记, 人工通道, 检票, 停止检票, 护照, 现金, 拒收现金, 改签. CHECK BEFORE YOU TRAVEL: (1) Visa-free still valid on your entry date (currently ends 24:00 on 31 Dec 2026, max 30 days): https://nl.china-embassy.gov.cn/eng/ls/zytz/ and FAQ https://nl.china-embassy.gov.cn/eng/ls/fhqz/202511/t20251110_11750419.htm . (2) Ordinary Dutch passport valid for the whole stay (at least 3 months if using 240-hour transit): https://en.nia.gov.cn/n147418/n147463/c183412/content.html . (3) Arrival card online, free, official channels only: https://s.nia.gov.cn/ArrivalCardFillingPC/ (notice https://nl.china-embassy.gov.cn/eng/ls/zytz/202511/t20251126_11760675.htm). (4) Staying with family: you or your host must register your stay within 24 hours of arrival; online (NIA 12367 app or mini program) the host normally files it, or register at the local police station: https://en.nia.gov.cn/n147418/n147468/c237295/content.html . (5) Payments: install Alipay and WeChat, link a Visa or Mastercard, verify your passport, and check fees and limits in the app: https://english.shanghai.gov.cn/en-Individuals-BankingandPayments-Payments/20260921/c2c94d06a0454c8fa05386b80d0ae865.html and https://www.tencent.com/tencent-announces-three-initiatives-to-make-inbound-payments-for-international-visitors-easier-than-ever-during-apec-2026/ . (6) Carry some RMB in small notes; merchants may not refuse cash (RMB is legal tender under Art. 16 of the PBOC Law, and detailed cash-acceptance rules apply since 1 Feb 2026): https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/202512/content_7055739.htm . (7) Trains: register on 12306 and verify your passport before the trip, and allow time for the staffed lane: https://www.12306.cn/en/ and https://www.12306.cn/en/faq.html . (8) Dutch travel advice (colour code, blocked apps, emergency numbers, embassy contacts), and whether it changed after the 22 Oct 2026 Tibet earthquake: https://www.nederlandwereldwijd.nl/reisadvies/china . (9) Mobile data, roaming or eSIM: check your operator's China terms (not verified here). (10) Save the emergency numbers: 110 police, 119 fire, 120 ambulance. (11) Install the learning app and download its offline content before you leave; its web address may not load in China. (12) Carry your passport at all times; it is also your train ticket.

facts.question: Can a Dutch (Netherlands) ordinary-passport holder enter mainland China without a visa today? Since when, for how many days and for which purposes?
facts.answer: Yes. Under China's unilateral visa-exemption policy, Dutch citizens with a valid ordinary passport may enter mainland China without a visa for business, tourism, family visits (visiting relatives and friends), exchange visits and transit, and stay up to 30 days per entry. The Netherlands has been covered since 00:00 on 1 December 2023 (Beijing time). The first trial allowed 15 days (business, tourism, family visits, transit) and was extended in May 2024 to 31 December 2025, still with 15 days. From 30 November 2024 the stay became 30 days and 'exchange visits' became an allowed purpose. The Chinese Embassy in the Netherlands' notice of 4 November 2025 extends the policy until 24:00 on 31 December 2026 (Beijing time). Visiting a partner's family falls under 'family visit'. Work, study and news reporting are not covered and still need a visa.

facts.question: What is the current end date of the visa-free policy for the Netherlands, and has an extension beyond it been announced (status 2026-11-02)?
facts.answer: As of 2 November 2026: with an ordinary Dutch passport you can enter China visa-free until 24:00 Beijing time on 31 December 2026. That end date comes from the extension China's Foreign Ministry announced on 3 November 2025, which the Chinese Embassy in the Netherlands published on 4 November 2025. As of 2 November 2026, no extension for the Netherlands beyond 31 December 2026 had been announced. Searches in English, Chinese and Dutch found none. A separate extension to 31 December 2027, announced by China's Foreign Ministry on 20 May 2026, covers Russian citizens only. It does not apply to Dutch passport holders. The last extension for the Netherlands came on 3 November 2025, about two months before the old end date. An earlier one came in May 2024. So there is no fixed pattern for when a decision comes. Until a new notice appears, assume you need a visa for any entry on or after 1 January 2027. If a visa-free stay starting in December 2026 would run into 2027, ask the embassy before you book. A new notice could appear at any time, so check the embassy's notices again before you book and before you fly.

facts.question: How are the 30 visa-free days counted, and what else must a visa-free entrant know (number of entries, passport, documents, longer stays)?
facts.answer: As of 2 November 2026, according to the visa-free FAQs of Chinese embassies, consulates and local governments (latest versions from 2025-2026): (1) Each visa-free stay may last up to 30 days. The 30 days are counted from the day after you arrive and run for 30 calendar days in a row: if you arrive on 1 March, you may stay until the end of 31 March. Leaving a day early gives you a margin for delays. (2) There is currently no limit on the number of visa-free entries or on total days of stay, but what you do in China must match the purpose of your visit. (3) The exemption is for holders of a valid ordinary passport travelling for business, tourism, visiting family or friends, exchange visits or transit. Your passport must be valid for your whole trip in China. Other purposes, such as work, study or journalism, are not covered and need a visa. (4) Carrying proof of your purpose is recommended, such as an invitation letter, your air tickets and accommodation bookings. (5) If you already plan to stay longer than 30 days, get the matching visa before you travel. If, after a visa-free entry, you have good reasons to stay longer, you must apply for a stay permit at the local public security exit-entry office. Overstaying is illegal: it brings a warning or, in serious cases, a fine of CNY 500 per day (up to CNY 10,000) or 5 to 15 days' detention (Exit and Entry Administration Law, Art. 78). (6) If you need a visa instead, Chinese visa offices in the Netherlands do not take fingerprints from applicants for short-term visas (stays of up to 180 days) until 31 December 2026 (notice of 19 December 2025).

facts.question: What is the 240-hour visa-free transit policy (conditions, ports), and does it apply to Dutch passport holders?
facts.answer: Yes, the Netherlands is on the list. Since 20 August 2026 the policy covers 57 countries; Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam were added then, and the count was 55 after Indonesia joined in June 2025. 40 of the 57 are European, including the Netherlands. Conditions from the National Immigration Administration (NIA): an ordinary passport valid for at least 3 months; an onward interline ticket with a confirmed date and seat to a third country or region, leaving within 240 hours (10 days); entry through one of 65 designated ports in 24 provincial-level regions, then staying within the permitted areas; completing the arrival card and cooperating with checks. There were 60 ports until 5 November 2025, when five Guangdong ports were added. The 240 hours run from 00:00 on the day after entry. Short-term tourism, business, visits and family visits are allowed; work, study and journalism still need a visa. Separately, any nationality may make a 24-hour direct transit if they stay in the port's restricted area. For a Dutch citizen the 30-day unilateral exemption is normally easier: the embassy notices state no third-country onward-ticket condition and no designated-port or area restriction for it. The 240-hour scheme matters mainly if the unilateral policy lapses. The 240-hour scheme started on 17 December 2024, replacing the 72- and 144-hour schemes; it then covered 54 countries and 60 ports in 24 provincial-level regions, and allowed travel between those regions (CCTV, reporting the NIA announcement).

facts.question: Is there an online arrival card, and how do foreigners complete it?
facts.answer: Yes. Since 20 November 2025 foreigners can submit their arrival-card information online before travelling, free of charge. Channels: the NIA website (the Chinese Embassy in the Netherlands gives https://s.nia.gov.cn/ArrivalCardFillingPC/), the NIA government service platform, the 'NIA 12367' app, or the NIA WeChat/Alipay mini programs, or by scanning the official QR code. Travellers who have not done it can still do it on arrival by scanning a QR code, at on-site self-service devices, or on a paper arrival card, which remains available. Seven groups are exempt, including holders of a Foreign Permanent Resident ID card, Hong Kong/Macao travel-permit holders, group-visa travellers, 24-hour direct-transit passengers, same-ship cruise passengers, e-channel users and foreign transport crew. NIA warns that scam sites imitate the service and charge fees; use only the official channels.

facts.question: Is a customs health declaration still required on entry?
facts.answer: No, not as a routine form. As of 2 November 2026, travellers entering China do not have to fill in a health declaration form. China's customs (GACC) dropped the entry/exit health declaration form from 1 November 2023, and 2026 travel guides report that it has not come back. You must still report to customs yourself on arrival if you have symptoms of an infectious disease (such as fever, cough, breathing difficulty, vomiting, diarrhoea, a rash or unexplained bleeding under the skin) or have been diagnosed with one, and cooperate with checks such as temperature and medical screening. Under the revised Frontier Health and Quarantine Law (in force since 1 January 2025), customs may ask any traveller to declare their health status truthfully and may check temperature. A false declaration or refusing a check can bring a warning or a fine of up to CNY 10,000 (CNY 10,000-50,000 in serious cases). Rules can change quickly when there is an outbreak, so check shortly before you fly.

facts.question: Must a foreign visitor register their accommodation, e.g. when staying in a private home with a partner's family instead of a hotel?
facts.answer: Yes. Under Article 39 of China's Exit and Entry Administration Law, hotels register their foreign guests, so a hotel guest has nothing extra to do. When a foreigner stays anywhere other than a hotel, such as the home of a partner's family, the foreigner or the host must register the stay with the local public security organ within 24 hours of arrival. Registration is done at the local police station, or at a police office or foreigner service station where one exists. Foreigners who entered visa-free must also register. Failing to register can lead to a warning and a fine of up to CNY 2,000 (Article 76).

facts.question: Can the accommodation registration for a private-home stay be done online (2026)?
facts.answer: Yes. It has been available nationwide since 21 September 2026 (NIA), after a pilot from 20 March 2026 in Hebei, Liaoning, Zhejiang, Hubei, Guangxi, Chongqing and Sichuan; before that, some places such as Beijing, Shanghai, Hainan and Chongqing ran their own online systems. Channels: the NIA government service platform website, the 'NIA 12367' app, the 'NIA 12367' WeChat mini program, or the Alipay mini program. Online registration has the same legal effect as registering at the police station, and in-person registration at the local police remains available. The host, who knows the residence details, normally files the first registration. A foreigner may file alone only when re-registering at a residence already registered on the platform, or when living in their own property. If online registration fails, go to the local police station in person. A registration record can be looked up afterwards, and the NIA 12367 hotline answers questions.

facts.question: Can foreigners link foreign Visa/Mastercard cards to Alipay and WeChat Pay, and since when?
facts.answer: Yes. Both apps let overseas users link international cards without a mainland Chinese bank account. The broad opening dates from July 2023: WeChat Pay (Weixin Pay) announced it on 20 July 2023 and Alipay on 21 July 2023. On 22 July 2023 Beijing's government listed Visa, Diners Club, Mastercard and JCB for WeChat, and Visa, Diners Club, Mastercard and Discover for Alipay. A more limited opening was reported by Reuters on 6 November 2019. Current lists: Ant Group (March 2025) names Visa, Mastercard, American Express, JCB, Discover, Diners Club International and UnionPay International for Alipay. Shanghai's government (2026) lists Visa, Mastercard, American Express, JCB, Discover and Diners Club International for Weixin Pay. Alipay no longer requires a prepaid account or a Chinese phone number.

facts.question: Can Alipay+ partner wallets or PayPal be used instead (relevant for a Dutch traveller)?
facts.answer: As of 2 Nov 2026: Some foreign e-wallets can pay in mainland China, and each network gives its own count. Chinese press reports in the run-up to the APEC meeting in Shenzhen (2026) put the number at 60, now including wallets from Japan, Korea, Europe and America, but none are named. UnionPay says over 200 overseas e-wallets from 37 countries and regions can scan to pay in mainland China. No source names a Dutch wallet. PayPal: since 11 Aug 2026, PayPal users in the US can pay at Weixin Pay merchants by QR code (PayPal World with Tencent's TenPay Global). Tencent says other markets will follow in phases, but no date for Europe or the Netherlands has been announced. For a Dutch traveller the practical route is still a Visa or Mastercard linked to Alipay and/or Weixin Pay.

facts.question: Is cash (RMB) still accepted, and may merchants refuse it (People's Bank of China rules)?
facts.answer: Yes, cash is legal tender and must be accepted. The 'Regulations on RMB Cash Receipt and Payment Services' (人民币现金收付及服务规定) were issued in December 2025 as PBOC / NDRC / NFRA Announcement [2025] No. 29 and have been in force since 1 February 2026. Fee-collecting bodies and businesses may not refuse cash (except where the law requires non-cash payment), may not ask or induce others to refuse it, and may not discriminate against cash payment. Businesses with staffed checkouts or face-to-face service must accept cash and keep reasonable change. Anyone refused can keep evidence and complain to the local PBOC branch or through city hotlines, and penalised violators are publicly named. Refusing cash was already prohibited before: Article 16 of the Law on the People's Bank of China and Article 3 of the RMB Administration Regulations make the renminbi legal tender that no unit or individual may refuse for any public or private debt in China, and the PBOC has run campaigns against cash refusal since 2018. Practical note: mobile QR payment is the norm, so carry some small RMB notes as a backup rather than as the main way to pay.

facts.question: Can foreign cards be used directly at hotels or big merchants, and at ATMs?
facts.answer: Partly. A PBOC / MOFCOM / SAFE notice of May 2024 requires key venues and merchants (e.g. shopping districts, chain supermarkets, restaurants, duty-free shops) to be able to take mobile payment, domestic and overseas bank cards, and cash. SAFE says foreign cards work on POS terminals at airports, hotels and large commercial areas, but also that foreign cards are still not widely accepted. For cash, bank-branch ATMs accept Visa and Mastercard for RMB withdrawals where the network logo is shown. Withdrawals with overseas cards are generally limited to RMB 3,000 per transaction (Shanghai government, Sept 2026), and the card issuer may set its own limits and fees.

facts.question: How does a foreigner buy train tickets with a passport on 12306 (English website/app), and how is the passport verified?
facts.answer: As of 2 November 2026: Buy on China Railway's official 12306 website (www.12306.cn/en, in English since November 2020) or the Railway 12306 app, which also has an English version (travel guides say the English has rough edges). Register with your passport and enter your details exactly as on the passport's data page. 12306's own registration rules say: type your name in passport order, keep any spaces inside your surname or given names, and put a space between surname and given names. You cannot buy tickets until your identity has been verified. Since 28 November 2023 you can do this online: enter your name, nationality and passport number for automatic verification, or upload a photo of the passport data page (guides say also a photo of you holding the passport) for manual review. Manual review can take several days (a 2024 China News Service report and a Trip.com guide both say 3-5 working days), so verify well before your trip. You can also verify in person with your passport at a station ticket window. Payment: Beijing's government says 12306 accepts Chinese or foreign bank cards and mobile payment apps. When the English site launched in 2020, reports said it took Chinese bank cards, Alipay and WeChat Pay, plus Visa, Mastercard, JCB and Diners Club cards. Travel guides report that foreign cards are often declined on 12306 and that American Express is not accepted. Bring the same physical passport you booked with: you need it to enter and leave the station.

facts.question: Besides 12306 online: station counters and Trip.com?
facts.answer: As of 2 November 2026: At the station, staffed ticket windows sell tickets when you show your passport (Shanghai government, 2024; Hunan provincial government, June 2026). Trip.com, a commercial agency, sells China train tickets in English at the same base fares as 12306. Guides disagree on whether Trip.com adds a service fee per ticket and how much, so check the total before you pay. 12306 itself charges no booking fee. Beijing's government (December 2025) advises buying only through China Railway's official platforms, the 12306 website or app, and a Shanghai government page notes that the railway does not handle problems with tickets bought through other websites.

facts.question: Can a foreign passport be used at the automatic station/ticket gates, or must foreigners use staffed lanes (any change 2024-2026)?
facts.answer: As of 2 November 2026 this still varies by station. Official guides say foreign travellers can enter and exit through automatic or manual ticket gates with the original passport used to buy the ticket (Beijing's expat guide, 2024; repeated in Hunan's provincial government guide, June 2026). Shanghai's government (January 2024) says you can swipe your passport at the automatic check-in machines or show it at the manual gate. In practice, sources disagree. One 2026 travel guide says major stations such as Beijing South and Shanghai Hongqiao have passport-reading gates, while older and conventional-rail stations may not. Others (Ctrip's Chinese booking terms, Trip.com, and guides for Chengdu and Zhangjiajie) say passports mostly don't work at the automatic gates and passport holders should use the staffed lane. Holders of China's Foreign Permanent Resident ID card have been able to use the self-service gates since late 2023; tourists do not have this card. No national railway announcement from 2025 or 2026 about passports at automatic gates was found. Practical rule: carry the same physical passport you booked with, try the gate if it has a passport reader, and otherwise go to the staffed lane, 人工通道 (réngōng tōngdào).

facts.question: Are train tickets electronic, and how does a passport holder get a receipt/invoice?
facts.answer: Yes. China's railways use paperless e-tickets, and you board with the passport used for booking; no paper ticket is needed. An e-invoice can be obtained in the Railway 12306 app or at station windows and self-service machines within 180 days after the trip ends. Passport users can also get e-invoices. Background from CCTV: rail e-invoices started on 1 November 2024; you request one from your own 12306 account within 180 days after the trip ends (or after paying a refund or change fee), so a paper ticket is no longer needed for expense claims. Since 1 October 2025 rail passenger transport uses e-invoices across the board, and a paper itinerary slip (纸质行程信息提示单) is still available.

facts.question: Is mobile data on a foreign roaming SIM or travel eSIM subject to the 'Great Firewall'?
facts.answer: As of 2 Nov 2026. Blocked services: no official or operator source found today says whether Google, WhatsApp and similar services work on roaming data or a travel eSIM in mainland China. Only eSIM sellers' guides address it. They say it depends on how the provider routes your data: plans that send your traffic out through a network outside mainland China (for example Singapore) usually let Google and WhatsApp load without a VPN, while a local Chinese SIM does not. Their claims differ, though: one seller says Google is blocked even with its eSIM, and plans routed through Hong Kong may still block some apps. On hotel, café or airport Wi-Fi in China these services stay blocked. Whether roaming on your Dutch SIM gets around the blocks could not be confirmed today. Costs: China is outside the EU 'roam like at home' area. An answer on KPN's customer forum says data use outside the EU needs a separate bundle, or costs can rise quickly. KPN and Vodafone NL offer roaming bundles that include China. Vodafone NL says that outside the EU your data stops at a limit of €60.50 (incl. VAT) unless you raise it, and a KPN customer reported on KPN's forum reaching €60.50 within minutes of arriving in China. Before you go, check your own operator's China bundle and your eSIM seller's routing, and test your apps after landing.

facts.question: What is the legal status of VPNs for travellers in mainland China?
facts.answer: As of 2 Nov 2026: under Chinese rules, networks may connect to the international internet only through the state telecom network's international gateways. The State Council's 1996 provisions (amended 1997) say no organisation or individual may set up or use other channels for international connections (Art. 6). The police can order the connection stopped, give a warning, fine up to CNY 15,000 and confiscate illegal income (Art. 14). The 1998 implementing measures say individual users must connect through an access network and 'not by other means'; the police can fine an individual up to CNY 5,000 for breaking this (Art. 12 and 22). A January 2017 notice from China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) names VPNs: without the telecom regulator's approval, no one may set up or rent dedicated lines, including VPNs, or other channels for cross-border business. MIIT said this mainly targets unlicensed companies or individuals that use international lines or VPNs to run cross-border telecom services. No official source found today says how these rules are applied to short-term foreign visitors. In today's check the Dutch travel advice gave no guidance on VPNs, but it warns that the authorities may check your phone or laptop for messages, including messages you have shared, on arrival and during your trip. This app gives no advice on VPN use.

facts.question: Which apps does a traveller need (verified core set)?
facts.answer: As of 2 Nov 2026, install these before you go: (1) Alipay and WeChat (Weixin Pay) to pay. Foreign visitors can link an international Visa or Mastercard. Small payments need no ID details; for larger amounts you must verify your identity in the app (see the payments cards). (2) Railway 12306, China Railway's official app and website (www.12306.cn/en). Its English version lets passport holders register, buy, change and refund tickets. (3) NIA 12367, the National Immigration Administration's app, also available as WeChat and Alipay mini programs. Use it, or the NIA website, for the free online arrival card, available since 20 Nov 2025; use official channels only, because fake sites exist. Use it also for accommodation registration when you stay somewhere other than a hotel, such as your partner's family's home: this must be done within 24 hours of your arrival there. Online registration has been available nationwide since 21 Sep 2026 and has the same legal effect as registering in person at the local police station, which is still possible. The NIA says your host should do the first online registration, or help you with it; you can file on your own only when registering again at an address you registered before through the NIA platform, or when staying in a home owned by you or your spouse in China. Not registering can lead to a warning or a fine.

facts.question: Ride-hailing (DiDi or via an Alipay mini program), maps (Amap/Baidu Maps in English), translator and Pleco: what is available?
facts.answer: As of 2 Nov 2026. Taxis: the Hunan provincial government's guidance for foreign visitors (June 2026) says the international version of the DiDi app lets foreigners register with a foreign phone number and an international credit card and book rides, and that rides can also be booked through mini programs in Alipay (tap 'Transport', then 'Taxi') and WeChat. Beijing's official 2024 guide also lists DiDi as a mini program inside Alipay. Maps: Amap (Gaode), Alibaba's map app, has an English version, which added ride-hailing for foreign visitors in more than 360 cities. SCMP (press) reported that sign-up initially accepted mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau phone numbers, so check whether it accepts your Dutch number. Google is blocked in China (Dutch travel advice), so do not count on Google Maps or Google Translate. Translation: Alipay has a built-in translator: tap 'Translation' on its home screen and type, speak or take a photo; it supports 16 languages (official Chinese guidance, 2024). Dictionary: Pleco for iPhone/iPad and Android; the basic version is free and includes the CC-CEDICT dictionary. Pleco says that once its dictionaries and add-ons are downloaded it works without an internet connection, so download them before you go. The Android version can also be installed directly from pleco.com/getandroid.

facts.question: Where are the Dutch embassy and consulates in mainland China, and how do you reach Dutch consular help?
facts.answer: As of 1 Nov 2026, the Dutch government lists one embassy and two consulates-general in mainland China. Embassy of the Netherlands, Beijing: Liangmahe South Road no. 4, Chaoyang District, 100600 Beijing; phone +86 10 85 32 02 00. Consulate-General, Guangzhou: Teem Tower, floor 34, Tianhe Road no. 208, 510620 Guangzhou; phone +86 20 38 13 22 00; its consular district is Guangdong, Guangxi, Fujian and Hainan. Consulate-General, Shanghai: Dawning Center Tower B, floor 10, Hongbaoshi Road no. 500, Changning District, 201103 Shanghai; phone +86 21 22 08 72 88; its district is Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Anhui. The embassy in Beijing covers all other provinces and regions, including central and south-west China (for example Hunan, Hubei, Jiangxi, Henan, Sichuan, Chongqing, Guizhou and Yunnan). A separate Consulate-General for Hong Kong and Macao is in Hong Kong, which is outside the mainland. The Dutch consulate-general in Chongqing has closed, although some older directories still list it. In an emergency, day or night, call the 24/7 contact centre of the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs (NederlandWereldwijd) on +31 247 247 247. If you have a Chinese phone number, you can call the embassy's local number instead and pay only the local rate. The official advice also gives a WhatsApp number, +31 857 737 400, but it says WhatsApp is always blocked in China, so phone if you can.

facts.question: What is the Dutch government's current travel advice for China (colour code, key warnings)?
facts.answer: As of 1 Nov 2026, the Dutch government's travel advice for China has colour code yellow: you can travel, but there are particular safety risks. The current version was last changed on 28 Aug 2026 and was still valid on 1 Nov 2026. Check nederlandwereldwijd.nl/reisadvies/china again just before you leave. Main warnings: You may not use, possess or sell drugs in China, including soft drugs. Penalties are much heavier than in the Netherlands, up to a heavy prison sentence or even the death penalty. Police test blood, urine or hair, and a positive test counts even if you took the drug before you arrived in China. As a foreigner you can be arrested for unclear or political reasons, for example on suspicion of spying or of endangering national security, and the Dutch embassy can then give little or no help. Posting or sharing messages that criticise China or its government can be punishable, even messages from before your trip, and officials can check your phone or laptop on arrival and during your trip. Do not photograph or film demonstrations, government buildings, military sites, the army or the police. Avoid demonstrations and large gatherings: if you are present at a demonstration you can be arrested for endangering national security. Watch out for pickpockets and theft, especially in crowded places. Also be wary of friendly English-speaking 'guides' or strangers who invite you to a tea shop, massage parlour or bar: you are likely to get a very high bill and may be forced, under threat of violence, to pay it. Hurricanes (typhoons) and tropical storms hit the coastal provinces mainly from May to November. In the south, heavy rain falls mainly from February to October and can cause floods, landslides and mudflows. Earthquakes are a risk mainly in the west of the country. The advice also reports a sudden flood on 26 Aug 2026 in Tibet near the Nepal border and warns of new flood waves there, often with little or no warning. To visit Tibet you need an entry permit, applied for through your tour operator, and the authorities sometimes refuse it. The government can temporarily block phone and internet traffic, and Google, Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, YouTube, X and many Dutch and international news media are always blocked. You must register within 24 hours of arrival. facts.question: Must a foreign visitor carry their passport at all times in mainland China?
facts.answer: Yes. As of 2 November 2026, Article 38 of China's Exit and Entry Administration Law (in force since 1 July 2013) says foreigners aged 16 or over who are staying in China must carry their passport or other international travel document, or their Chinese stay or residence permit, and let the police (public security) check it. Refusing a police check of your documents can bring a warning and possibly a fine of up to CNY 2,000 (Art. 76). Hotels must register foreign guests with the police. If you stay in a private home, for example with your partner's family, you or your host must register you with the local police within 24 hours of moving in. Not doing so can also bring a warning and possibly a fine of up to CNY 2,000 (Art. 39 and 76).

facts.question: Did the 2026 State Council provisions on exit and entry change anything for visa-free visitors (truthful purpose, questioning, penalties)?
facts.answer: As of 2 November 2026: China's State Council Provisions on Exit and Entry Administration (国务院关于出境入境管理的规定, State Council Order No. 841, dated 22 July 2026, published 31 July 2026, in force since 15 September 2026) do not change the visa-free rules, but they spell out how checks work. The reason you give for entering and staying must be true and lawful. Immigration and visa officers may ask you questions and require you to show or provide documents, materials and electronic data (电子数据), and you must cooperate. Whoever writes an invitation letter for you is responsible for its truth and must help the authorities verify it (Art. 3). A traveller who gives false materials or makes false statements can be refused entry (Art. 3). A foreigner who does so when applying for a Chinese visa abroad or for entry at a border port can be barred from entering China for 1 to 5 years (Art. 5). A person who issues a false invitation letter or other false application material for someone else can be fined CNY 5,000-10,000, and an organisation CNY 10,000-50,000 (Art. 11). For a Dutch visitor entering visa-free to see a partner's family: state the real purpose (visiting family, or tourism), carry proof such as your return ticket and your hosts' address or an invitation letter, and answer border questions truthfully.
